summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Patient access to their electronic health records (EHRs) could improve care and reduce errors by enabling patient contribution to documentation. However, interactive functions that support such engagement remain underresearched. <strong>Objective:</strong> The purpose of this study was to analyze patients’ use of the free-text comment function in the Swedish national patient-accessible EHR. <strong>Methods:</strong> Comments made by patients between 2015 and 2021 for health care professionals to view were retrieved from the patient-accessible EHR administration service in Sweden. The number and length of comments were analyzed using descriptive statistics and chi-square tests, while the content was examined qualitatively using inductive content analysis. In addition, comments were coded for sentiment (positive, neutral, or negative) and note content, and users were classified according to whether they had submitted at least 1 comment referring to mental health care. <strong>Results:</strong> A total of 1670 comments were left by 659 patients, of which 15 had irrelevant content (15/1670, 0.9%; 95% CI 0.4%-1.4%), leaving 1655 comments for analysis. Most comments (948/1655, 57.3%; 95% CI 54.9%-59.7%) were related to matters other than note content, and nearly all had a neutral (920/1655, 55.6%; 95% CI 53.2%-58.0%) or negative (702/1655, 42.4%; 95% CI 40.0%-44.8%) sentiment. Patients who submitted a comment referencing mental health care tended to leave more comments overall (median 7 vs 2 comments per patient), and their comments were more frequently negative than comments written by other patients (313/495, 63.2% vs 389/1160, 33.5%; <i>P</i><.001). The most prevalent categories were care engagement, perceived inaccuracies, complaints, and requests. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> Patient engagement with clinical notes has the potential to enhance documentation accuracy and strengthen patient-clinician communication. To realize these benefits safely, such features must be deliberately designed and clearly explained to users to avoid patient safety risks and unnecessary burdens on health care professionals.
title: Patient Use of a Comment Function in Electronic Health Records: Mixed Methods Case Study

summary: Background: Engagement with suicide-related content online is often assumed to be harmful, yet many individuals with lived experience describe such content as supportive or even life-preserving. Despite policy and clinical concerns, little is known about how people intentionally or unintentionally encounter this content, how they interpret it, and how these experiences shape perceived harm or benefit. Objective: This study aims to explore how intent and context influence the ways in which individuals with lived experience of suicidality encounter, interpret, and respond to suicide-related online content, and to identify factors associated with perceived harm and benefit. Methods: An exploratory cross-sectional survey was conducted with a convenience sample of 713 UK-based participants aged 16 to 60 years and older, 95.9% (n=684) of whom reported having lived experience of suicidality. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics, including chi-square tests, to examine associations between engagement patterns, intent, and suicidality. Free-text responses were coded using content analysis to identify categories relating to motivations for engagement, emotional responses, and perceived impact. Results: Participants reported a broad range of experiences. While 30.0% (214/713) described suicide-related content as contributing to suicidal thoughts or attempts, others reported relief, validation, or reduced feelings of isolation, with 21.0% (150/713) attributing content to preventing an attempt. Clear differences emerged between participants who actively sought out content (“seekers”) and those who encountered it unintentionally (“stumblers”). Seekers more frequently reported positive or understanding responses, often in the context of unmet offline support needs, whereas stumblers were more likely to report shock or distress. Approximately 39.9% (151/378) of participants described their engagement as neither intentional nor accidental, potentially reflecting a blurred boundary between passive exposure and active seeking, as well as the difficulty individuals face in accurately identifying and articulating their own motivations in relation to suicidality. Conclusions: Engagement with suicide-related online content cannot be characterized as uniformly harmful. Outcomes depend on user intent, emotional state, and the context of engagement, and they may change over time. Clinical, regulatory, and policy approaches should move beyond risk-only frameworks to account for the nuanced and sometimes supportive roles such content plays in how individuals make sense of suicidal thoughts, while still protecting those at risk.
title: Navigating Suicide-Related Online Content in Individuals With Lived Experience of Suicidality: Cross-Sectional Survey

summary: Background: Patients with cancer frequently experience complex and multidimensional symptom burdens. Standardized patient-reported outcome measures provide structured approaches to symptom assessment but may not capture the full range of symptom-related and psychosocial concerns expressed in patients’ narratives. Patient-generated social media data offer a complementary source for examining how these concerns are expressed online. Objective: This study aimed to characterize cancer symptom–related narratives in Chinese social media posts using a conventional symptom assessment framework and to identify additional experiential themes through neural topic modeling. Methods: A computational text analysis integrating large language model (LLM) annotation and neural topic modeling was conducted. A corpus of 26,086 first-person patient narratives was collected from Xiaohongshu and Zhihu between November 2013 and February 2026 using cancer-related search terms. First-person narratives and 6 SPPADE (sleep disturbance, pain, physical function impairment, anxiety, depression, and low energy or fatigue) symptom domains were identified using GPT-4o-mini (OpenAI) and validated against independent human coding. Symptom occurrence, co-occurrence, multiplicity, and coping strategies were characterized, with exploratory stratified analyses by cancer type. BERTopic modeling was applied to identify latent themes, platform sensitivity analyses, and temporal distribution were examined. Results: For first-person narrative identification, human raters showed 89.2% agreement (Cohen κ=0.784); the LLM achieved an -score of 81.2% against the adjudicated reference standard. For SPPADE extraction, mean Cohen κ values for LLM-human agreement were 0.714 (SD 0.114) and 0.754 (SD 0.095) across the 6 symptom domains. Overall, 13,896 of 26,086 (53.3%) posts contained at least 1 identifiable symptom. Pain was the most frequently identified symptom (5783/26,086, 22.2%), followed by physical function impairment (4153/26,086, 15.9%) and depression (4050/26,086, 15.5%). Pain and physical function impairment formed the most frequent co-occurring symptom pair (n=1407). Coping strategies were described in 7104/26,086 (27.2%) posts; medication-based approaches were most prominent, particularly for pain and sleep disturbance, while social and psychological support were more common for anxiety and depression. BERTopic modeling identified 13 latent themes, including cancer treatment trajectories, health care system interaction, existential distress, family involvement, and financial burden, highlighting experiential concerns that may be underrepresented in conventional symptom assessment. The proportion of posts containing at least 1 SPPADE symptom was similar between Xiaohongshu and Zhihu (53.2% vs 54.1%; =.35), although individual symptom distributions differed across platforms. Conclusions: Chinese social media posts contained multidimensional symptom-related narratives alongside psychosocial and experiential concerns that may be less visible in structured symptom assessment. Patient-generated social media data may therefore provide a complementary source for understanding cancer symptom experiences and supportive care concerns. However, differences in platform composition, uneven temporal coverage, and the nonrepresentativeness of social media users limit generalizability, and the clinical utility of integrating such data into routine symptom assessment requires further evaluation.
title: Characterizing Cancer Symptom Experiences and Related Psychosocial Concerns Through Chinese Social Media Narratives: Computational Text Analysis

summary: Background: Unemployment has economic consequences and is associated with emotional distress and impairment. Joblessness is often associated with depression, leading to a vicious cycle of reduced drive to seek work, deepening financial stress, and worsening depression. Few scalable interventions exist that integrate job-search strategies with cognitive behavioral techniques. Objective: The study aimed to determine the efficacy of a Distress-Informed Return-to-Work Intervention (DRIVEN). The primary hypothesis was that DRIVEN would be more efficacious than the control condition in improving job-search behavior. Secondary analyses examined job attainment, depression, and positive affect. Methods: A randomized controlled trial was conducted from August 2023 to September 2024. Assessments were at baseline, weeks 1 through 6, and 8 and 16 weeks postintervention. Participants were a nationwide sample of unemployed job seekers aged 18 years or older who had never earned more than US $100,000 in a year. Participants received either (1) DRIVEN, which included 6 weeks of cognitive behavioral exercises in a mobile app combined with three 1-hour coaching sessions over videoconference or (2) emailed articles containing job-search advice. Primary outcome measures were subscales of a modified Job Search Behavior Scale (preparatory and active job search). Secondary outcomes included job attainment and mental health outcomes. Results: Participants were a nationwide sample (N=126; mean age 33.6, SD 6.6 y), including 62 (49.2%) females. During the acute treatment phase, mixed-effects linear models showed that for DRIVEN, preparatory job-search behavior increased by an estimated 0.053 (95% CI 0.031-0.076) units per day from baseline, which was a larger effect than in the control condition (0.011, 95% CI −0.011 to 0.033 units per day; =.008). Active job-search behavior increased by 0.061 (95% CI 0.038-0.084) units per day from baseline, which was significantly larger than in the control group (point estimate: 0.025, 95% CI 0.001-0.047; =.03). Depression decreased more in the DRIVEN group vs control (DRIVEN point estimate=−0.214, 95% CI −0.255 to −0.172 vs control group point estimate=−0.122, 95% CI −0.163 to −0.081; =.002), and participants were more likely to get a job in the DRIVEN group (68.3% vs 50.8%; =.046). Self-report outcomes did not significantly differ during the follow-up periods. Conclusions: DRIVEN was superior to emailed job-search advice for the primary outcome (job-search behavior) and secondary outcomes (job attainment, depression, and positive affect). This intervention may be beneficial for distressed unemployed individuals seeking work. Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06026280; https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06026280 International Registered Report Identifier (IRRID): RR2-10.2196/62715
title: Job Coaching and Smartphone-Based Cognitive Behavioral Techniques for Returning to Work and Coping With Unemployment (DRIVEN): Randomized Controlled Trial

summary: Background: Clinical practice guidelines are central instruments of evidence-based care; yet, in many domains, particularly rare or complex diseases, multiple guidelines coexist and frequently offer conflicting advice. Existing strategies for resolving such divergences are often labor-intensive, opaque, and insufficiently reproducible. Objective: This tutorial aimed to develop and demonstrate a reproducible workflow for transforming divergent clinical guideline recommendations and literature-derived white areas into human-reviewed Delphi-ready candidate items. Methods: Following a step-by-step tutorial structure, we demonstrate the workflow using penile cancer as a worked example. The process comprises manual selection of clinical guidelines, a systematic PubMed search for literature-derived candidate issues potentially unaddressed by the selected guidelines, selection of 3 complementary large language models (LLMs), and execution of predefined prompts, multimodal recommendation extraction, semantic harmonization, and item-level guideline stance classification. The evaluative process combines a 3-LLM ensemble consistency check with an independent pre-Delphi appraisal by 4 penile cancer experts using a predefined 5-point suitability scale and acceptance threshold. Results: In the worked example in the field of penile cancer as a high-stakes use case, the workflow extracted 157 clinical recommendations from 5 guidelines and consolidated them into 68 harmonized guideline-derived items. Stance classification identified 15 uniformly supported items and 53 divergent, ambiguous, or incompletely addressed items. In parallel, literature processing generated 95 harmonized white-area items, of which 9 were classified as true white-area items not addressed by the included guidelines. The final methodological output was a set of 62 human-reviewed Delphi-ready candidate items for subsequent clinical consensus voting. Conclusions: This methodology provides a scalable, transparent, and transferable approach for identifying and structuring interguideline inconsistencies and evidence gaps. By combining LLM-assisted analysis with independent external expert appraisal, it supports the reproducible transformation of heterogeneous guideline content into Delphi-ready candidate items.
title: From Divergent Guidelines to Delphi-Ready Items: Tutorial for Large Language Model–Assisted Guideline Harmonization Using Penile Cancer as a Worked Example

summary: Pediatric health care systems face increasing uncertainty driven by rapid technological change, workforce shifts and shortages, environmental threats, and evolving family and community needs. Pediatrics requires future-focused considerations that go beyond adult systems, including family-centered care, developmental trajectories, and long-term societal impacts on child well-being. While the future cannot be predicted, futures medicine methods offer structured approaches to anticipate change and support proactive, values-driven planning. This Viewpoint describes the application of pediatric futures methods within an academic, independent nonprofit pediatric health system and proposes a practical framework that connects future readiness to strategic decision-making and daily care delivery. Futures medicine methods are not new in pediatric health care but may not be visible from the front line of care delivery, which provides an opportunity for clinical, operational, administrative, and enterprise leaders to implement these methods in their workflows. This paper introduces the discover to deliver pediatric futures framework, a continuum that links long-range futures discovery to near-term strategic planning, operational design, implementation, and outcome demonstration, emphasizing future methods and activities for applicable use.
title: Discover to Deliver Pediatric Futures: Viewpoints of Future Medicine From a Pediatric Health Care System

summary: Background: Voice disorders are common, yet access to timely specialist assessment is often limited. Automated analysis of short voice recordings may support early screening, but achieving robust performance on heterogeneous clinical datasets remains challenging. Objective: This study aims to investigate the impact of synthetic speech augmentation on voice disorder recognition and classification using the Saarbrücken Voice Database (SVD) and to develop an adaptive ensemble with learnable weighting and optional sex embedding. Methods: Sentence recordings from the SVD were used for binary voice disorder recognition (VDR, n=1988) and 4-class voice disorder classification (VDC; n=1199). Two text-to-speech (TTS) models, XTTS and Kartoffelbox, generated 1 synthetic sample for each training instance. Synthetic speech quality was assessed in a blinded listening evaluation with 40 samples per TTS model. Baseline models included support vector machine (SVM), ResNet-18, long short-term memory, and transformer-based architectures, including Hidden-Unit BERT (HuBERT), Wav2Vec 2.0, and WavLM. Ensemble learning and learnable fusion (LF), with and without a sex embedding (LFS), were evaluated using bootstrapped performance estimates and standard classification metrics. Area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) was reported for VDR. Results: In the blinded evaluation, Kartoffelbox-generated synthetic samples were less often identified as synthetic than XTTS-generated synthetic samples (10/19, 52.6% vs 17/19, 89.5%). In pooled original and synthetic ratings, Kartoffelbox showed higher pathological-status identification than XTTS for pathological samples (22/29, 75.9% vs 19/29, 65.5%) and nonpathological samples (8/10, 80.0% vs 6/10, 60.0%), as well as higher diagnostic-class assignment (20/39, 51.3% vs 14/39, 35.9%). Among the baseline models, HuBERT showed the most balanced VDR performance (accuracy=0.85, -score=0.84). Kartoffelbox-based augmentation further improved performance, with HuBERT achieving 0.88 sensitivity, 0.87 accuracy, and 0.85 -score. LF showed minor improvements in threshold-dependent metrics (accuracy=0.87, -score=0.86), while LFS further balanced sensitivity and specificity (accuracy=0.88, AUC=0.92). The equal-weight ensemble achieved the highest AUC among ensemble approaches (AUC=0.93). For VDC, HuBERT was the strongest baseline (accuracy=0.72, median -score=0.63), and LF achieved the highest overall fusion performance (accuracy=0.73, -score=0.66), while laryngitis remained one of the more challenging classes. Conclusions: High-quality synthetic speech augmentation can improve automated voice disorder analysis across heterogeneous clinical data, with effectiveness varying by the TTS model. Multimodel fusion of complementary architectures provided robust performance for screening and multiclass classification, with the strongest approach varying by metric and task. These findings support further evaluation of AI-assisted preassessment in clinical and telemedicine settings.
title: Detection of Pathological Voice Samples Using a Text-to-Speech–Inspired Approach With Multiple Model Architectures: Method Development and Comparative Evaluation Study
